I've been a loyal T-Mobile customer since 2016, when they first launched the T-Mobile ONE plan. I've been getting a military discount the whole time, but even with that, T-Mobile's price hikes have pushed my monthly bill to $113. I finally had enough and started looking for cheaper alternatives. On top of that, with the new Apple iPhone 18 Pro costing at least $100 more this year, I figured if I was going to upgrade my phone anyway, lowering my monthly bill could help offset that cost. So I started researching MVNOs.

What is an MVNO?

An MVNO stands for Mobile Virtual Network Operator. Simply put, an MVNO is a wireless carrier that doesn't own its own nationwide cellular network. Instead, they buy network capacity from one of the major carriers (AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon) and resell it to their own customers. Think of them as middlemen for wireless service.

Switching to an MVNO doesn't necessarily mean giving up the network you already use. For example, Mint Mobile runs on T-Mobile's network, Visible runs on Verizon's, and US Mobile lets you choose between all three major networks. I'll focus on these three MVNOs in this article because they were the ones I researched most extensively before leaving T-Mobile, but there are plenty of other options out there.

Put simply, an MVNO gives you another way to buy wireless service without dealing directly with the companies that own the networks.

Why are MVNOs cheaper? What are the catches?

If MVNOs use the same networks as AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon, how can they charge so much less? The simple answer is that MVNOs don't have to shoulder the costs of operating a nationwide wireless network. They don't build or maintain their own infrastructure, many operate primarily online without physical stores, and they tend to have smaller staff. The savings are passed on to customers in the form of lower monthly bills.

MVNO plans tend to be simpler, without the perks and add-ons that come with traditional major carriers. Depending on the carrier and plan, you might not get free streaming services or promotions designed to keep you locked in. But the money you save with an MVNO, if you actually want those "free" perks, can more than cover the cost of subscribing to them yourself.

This is exactly my situation. I've been using T-Mobile's free MLB.TV every baseball season, but I never watch Netflix, so the "Netflix on Us" promotion is useless to me. Even if I wanted both, paying for those subscriptions myself and subtracting what I save by switching would still leave money in my pocket. At the end of the day, what I really want is reliable, affordable wireless service, not a bundle of extras from T-Mobile that I don't need.

The so-called "catches" aren't about inferior service quality — they're about getting less. What exactly you give up depends on the MVNO and plan you choose. Video streaming might be limited to lower resolutions, high-speed or premium data allotments can vary, and network prioritization can differ. My home has very fast Wi-Fi, and I rarely go to concerts or sporting events where congestion is common, so network prioritization doesn't matter much for my daily use. But I do travel internationally sometimes, so international data is an important consideration for me. Some MVNOs include international data and texting, while others charge extra or have more limited coverage outside the US.

There are also some less obvious differences, especially when buying a new iPhone. If you choose an MVNO as your carrier, Apple Card monthly installments and the iPhone Upgrade Program won't be available to you. If you want to use either of those options, you're limited to AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon. Practically speaking, if you buy an iPhone directly from Apple, you typically have to pay for it all upfront. The major carriers usually offer generous trade-in deals and other promotions that MVNOs generally don't match. Not all MVNOs support Apple Watch, so if you use a cellular-connected Apple Watch, that's something to keep in mind.

Finally, most MVNOs rely more heavily on phone and online support rather than in-person staff at physical retail locations. I'm fairly tech-savvy and don't want to wait in line at a store for help anyway. And in my experience, store associates end up calling the same number to wait for the same people, so I can do that just as easily from home. For me, this isn't a big deal.

Most importantly, none of these are inherent limitations of MVNOs. Depending on the carrier and plan, so it's worth looking closely at exactly what you're getting before making the switch.

Three MVNOs worth considering

After deciding to leave T-Mobile, I started looking at alternatives. Verizon's and AT&T's postpaid plans were even more expensive than what I was already paying, so the other two major carriers were out. I narrowed my search to US Mobile, Mint Mobile, and Visible. Each had something appealing, and all of them could significantly lower my monthly bill without forcing me off a major carrier's network.

US Mobile is arguably the most flexible of the three, and it's the carrier I ultimately chose after leaving T-Mobile. But that doesn't mean it's necessarily the best fit for you, or that it's definitely the best MVNO of the three. It's simply the choice that worked best for me.

US Mobile wasn't actually my first choice. I hadn't heard of the company at all until I started researching MVNOs. But the more I looked at what it offers, the more it stood out. Here's why: US Mobile provides service on all three major US networks, letting customers pick the one that works best for them. It also offers a Multi-Network add-on that lets you activate two networks on the same iPhone simultaneously, without needing an extra phone number. Both networks are tied to the same line, so your iPhone can use whichever has a stronger signal for calls and data. That means if T-Mobile works well at your office but Verizon is better at home, you can use both without carrying two phones or managing two numbers. This US Mobile feature costs extra, and I personally don't need it, but it's nice that the option exists.

Having just moved to a new place, I wanted to see how Verizon's coverage compared to T-Mobile's in my new neighborhood, so I decided to test both networks myself. I set up my wife's iPhone on US Mobile's Light Speed network (T-Mobile) and mine on Warp (Verizon) so we could compare coverage firsthand. We found Verizon to be noticeably better in our area, making the switch to US Mobile a win-win: better coverage and a significantly lower monthly bill.

Mint Mobile was originally my top pick because it's owned by T-Mobile, meaning I could stay on the same network I was familiar with, but for a lot less money. What I didn't like was that it doesn't include international data. My wife and I love taking cruises — travel is a big part of our lives — so having cellular data outside the US is important to us. Mint does offer international data, but at an additional cost that quickly eats into the savings. I also didn't like how taxes and fees are billed separately.

Visible is similarly straightforward, but it only uses Verizon's network. My biggest hesitation with Visible was Verizon's coverage in my area. I'd been a T-Mobile customer for nearly a decade, so I knew exactly how T-Mobile's network performed, but I had no idea about Verizon's coverage. That was really the only thing that stopped me from picking Visible over US Mobile, because US Mobile let me try Verizon's network with T-Mobile and AT&T as backups in case Verizon didn't work out. Visible's top unlimited plan also comes with a free cellular Apple Watch plan, which is pretty appealing. (US Mobile's top plan on its Warp (Verizon) network offers the same perk.)

What you need to switch

Switching to an MVNO was even easier than I expected. My wife and I kept our existing iPhones, and moving both lines from T-Mobile to US Mobile took about ten minutes. I didn't even have to leave the couch. You'll need an unlocked, compatible iPhone (or Android phone, though I'm focusing on iPhones here), along with some information from your current carrier. If you want to keep your existing phone number, don't cancel your old service until the number transfer is complete.

Here's what you'll need to switch:

  • Your current carrier's account number
  • A transfer PIN
  • An unlocked, compatible iPhone
  • A new eSIM
  • A little patience

I prepaid a year of US Mobile's unlimited data plan for both lines in preparation for the switch. My wife doesn't use a cellular Apple Watch and doesn't care about video quality, so she chose US Mobile's Unlimited Starter plan, which saved $100 compared to the Unlimited Premium plan I picked. Both lines plus an Apple Watch line came to $500 for the year — far less than the $1,356 my wife and I were paying T-Mobile for two lines a year (with no Apple Watch service). (Again, that T-Mobile price already included a military discount!)

Getting a transfer PIN from T-Mobile was straightforward; I was half-expecting to run into an endless maze of complexity. Instructions for Verizon and AT&T are available [here].

Once my iPhone connected to Wi-Fi, US Mobile delivered a new eSIM straight to me, and installation was as simple as tapping a button in an email and following the on-screen prompts. The same process applied to my wife's iPhone. The only extra step was setting up my Apple Watch, which I handled easily through US Mobile's app.

Why I'm sticking with an MVNO

Same coverage, lower bill: For the amount I'm saving, the trade-offs have been well worth it. My home has fast Wi-Fi, so my cellular data needs aren't heavy (though in speed tests, US Mobile's speeds are just as fast as T-Mobile's were). What matters most to me is having a strong, stable cellular signal when I leave Wi-Fi — especially for making and receiving calls and texts.

No long-term contracts: Most carriers have already moved away from traditional contract plans in favor of device installment plans, which effectively do the same thing — keep you locked into their network until your device is paid off. I've always bought my iPhones directly from Apple because I want the freedom of owning an unlocked phone, but I appreciate that US Mobile, Mint, and Visible all don't require contracts.

Easy to switch: Most MVNOs let you pay month to month, so you're not tied down by long-term contracts. If one carrier has a great deal this month and another has a better deal next month, switching is quick and easy. Prepaid accounts also don't require credit checks, meaning switching won't ding your credit with a hard inquiry, nor will you be denied service based on your credit history the way you might with a postpaid account. My credit isn't bad, but I didn't want to leave a hard inquiry on my record from switching from T-Mobile to Verizon and take a hit to my credit score.

Zach Chadwick's top comment

I've been on T-Mobile since 2014. Two lines with Device Promotional Trade-in were $135 a month. After price hikes, new plan changes, and trade-in requirements, my bill climbed to $185 a month.

I switched to Visible in September 2025. I went with their Pro plan and used promo code SAVE26, getting their top plan for $33 a month for 26 months.

After my mom's trade-in credit ran out, I switched her too. They had a half-off annual deal at the time, putting their top plan at $275 for the year.

Our two lines together cost $671 this year — just four months of what my T-Mobile bill used to be.

I haven't run into any issues. I set up Autopay. They don't force you to use a debit card or checking account. I'm on 5G UW 90% of the time. I can stream 4K seamlessly with zero buffering.

I also set up a Visible "Circle" that lets you invite others and get $5 back per line, which I used to cover everyone's bill in the circle.

The annual savings really add up: There's a trade-off with flexibility — if you're willing to prepay for a full year of service, you can usually save quite a bit more. Most MVNOs offer significant discounts on annual plans, so you're trading the freedom to switch at any time for a lower overall price.

No surprise charges: As I mentioned earlier, my wife and I love taking cruises. If you've ever forgotten to put your iPhone in airplane mode and ended up connecting to the ship's cellular network, you know the bill can be terrifying. With a prepaid plan, I don't have to worry about accidentally racking up a huge roaming charge. If roaming isn't included in the plan, my phone simply won't connect to a foreign network and charge me. US Mobile's plans also include taxes and fees, so the price you see is the price you actually pay.

Switching to an MVNO isn't just about finding the cheapest service — it's about getting the service I actually need without paying for things I don't want or use. So far, I haven't missed anything (though I know I'll definitely miss that free MLB.TV). In fact, I now have an Apple Watch line that I didn't have before, but my bill is still lower than before. I'm using the same iPhones, the same phone numbers, coverage on US Mobile's Warp (Verizon) network is better than before in my area, and if I find a better option down the road, I still have the freedom to switch.

Your priorities may be different from mine, and MVNOs aren't for everyone. But if your wireless bill is high and you haven't considered an MVNO, it's worth a look. You might be surprised at how little you actually give up.
